title: Liberalism Is Worth Saving. Here’s How.
gist: In an excerpt from his new book, Nobel laureate economist Daron Acemoglu argues liberalism's establishment wing abandoned the working class through 'sins of omission and commission' — failing to address postindustrial economic dislocation while embracing elite-driven social engineering — and proposes a 'working-class liberalism' built on experimentation, nondomination, economic growth, and soft communitarianism as the only viable alternative to rising illiberal, antidemocratic movements.

themes.theme: Diagnosis: how establishment liberalism lost the working class

insights.claim: Liberalism succeeded initially by building institutions and delivering results, but once it became the political establishment it failed to adjust to postindustrial realities and, in Acemoglu's view, lost some of its own core values.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Frames the current crisis of liberal democracy as self-inflicted institutional drift rather than purely external attack — relevant for assessing the durability and reformability of liberal-democratic governance in major Western economies.
insights.quote: Estab­lishment liberalism did not adjust to new realities. Worse, liberals lost the plot and some of liberalism’s values together with it.

insights.claim: Acemoglu identifies a 'sin of omission': as the college-educated segment of society became more dominant within liberal politics, liberal democracies became less likely to seek solutions to the postindustrial economic challenges disproportionately afflicting the less-educated working class.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Identifies the demographic composition of liberal political coalitions (college-educated dominance) as a direct causal driver of policy neglect toward working-class economic concerns — relevant to understanding populist backlash dynamics across Western democracies.
insights.quote: Liberalism changed as the college-educated seg­ment of society became more dominant, and this made liberal democracies less likely to seek solutions to the postindustrial challenges that heavily afflicted the less educated.

insights.claim: The 'sin of commission' was that the postindustrial educated elite abandoned key liberal precepts — commitment to self-government, community, and shared prosperity — that were critical to liberal democracy's earlier success.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Argues the crisis is not just economic neglect but an active abandonment of foundational liberal values by elites, a distinct causal claim relevant to political-risk analysts assessing whether reform is a matter of policy or of values realignment.
insights.quote: The sin of commission was that the postindustrial educated elite abandoned many of the key precepts of liberalism, including the commitment to self-­government, community, and shared prosperity
insights.locator: The sin of commission was that

insights.claim: Automation eroded the natural pathways to shared prosperity and solidarity, regulation drifted away from those it was meant to protect, and social engineering intensified while turning away from foundational liberal values, together building a powerful backlash against liberalism.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Names three concrete mechanisms (automation's distributional effects, regulatory capture/drift, over-reaching social engineering) driving the populist backlash — a checklist for identifying which policy areas require reform to rebuild liberal legitimacy.
insights.quote: Automation eroded the natural pathways to shared prosperity and solidarity. Regulation drifted away from those it was meant to protect. Social engineering became more intense and turned its back on some of the foundational liberal values, building up a powerful backlash.

insights.claim: Acemoglu rejects the conclusion that liberalism has run its course and should be replaced by postliberal philosophies, arguing instead that liberalism is worth saving and remaking.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Positions the author against both establishment complacency and postliberal alternatives, staking out a reformist middle path relevant to debates over the future direction of center-left politics in Western democracies.
insights.quote: With these sins, perhaps liberalism has run its course and we should turn to postliberal philosophies for guidance. ... I disagree. Liberalism is worth saving and remaking.

themes.theme: The four pillars of a rebuilt liberalism

insights.claim: Acemoglu's proposed framework for renewed liberal institutions rests on four pillars: the vitality of experimentation (encouraging people to try new things to build technical and social knowledge), nondomination and self-government (how power should be organized), economic growth and its equitable sharing, and 'soft communitarianism' (making community integral to liberal democracy while balancing its effects on individual freedom).
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Provides a structured, four-part policy framework that could inform how center-left parties or policymakers redesign liberal governance platforms.
insights.quote: These are, 1) the vitality of experimentation... 2) nondomination and self-­government... 3) economic growth... and, 4) soft communitarianism
insights.locator: My theory leads to a number of conclusions

insights.claim: Acemoglu argues 'nondomination' — the idea that no state, individual, or group should have arbitrary power to restrict one's choices — is a more appropriate foundation for liberal freedom than classical liberalism's narrower concept of noninterference, because nondomination also requires basic social and economic security so people can actually experiment freely.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Reframes the philosophical basis for redistribution and public services (healthcare, infrastructure) as a requirement of freedom itself rather than a trade-off against it — relevant to debates over the scope of the welfare state within liberal political theory.
insights.quote: an individual who fears that they or their family will die of hunger if they are fired by their employer is in a situation of domination and could not be expected to experiment freely. Therefore, nondomination calls for some amount of redistribution and the provision of public services
insights.locator: Nondomination also assures some basic social

insights.claim: Economic growth is framed as self-reinforcing with experimentation — entrepreneurial and technical experimentation drives growth, and growth in turn expands the resources and options available for further experimentation and nondomination.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Positions economic growth not as separate from liberal values but as structurally intertwined with freedom and innovation — relevant to debates about whether growth-oriented and equity-oriented policy goals are complementary or in tension.
insights.quote: Experimenting with entrepreneurial endeavors, new production techniques, and new goods and services drives economic growth, and economic growth expands opportunities for experimentation.
insights.locator: Economic growth is essential for the betterment

insights.claim: Communities play an essential role because experimentation is nearly useless without social learning — if only the individual experimenter learns from an experiment, there is little contribution to collective knowledge, making trust and communication within communities central to a functioning liberal society.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Justifies why liberal governance should invest in community-level institutions and local self-government, not just individual rights protections — relevant to designing decentralized or localist policy interventions.
insights.quote: Experiments are nearly useless without social learning—if nobody other than the experimenter learns from them and changes their beliefs and practices, there will be little contribution to collective knowledge

themes.theme: Working-class liberalism as the practical program

insights.claim: Acemoglu labels the practical implementation of his liberal framework 'working-class liberalism,' emphasizing that this is not a defensive concession to avoid backlash but is rooted in the diagnosis that liberalism's failures stem directly from its abandonment of the working class and its priorities.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Distinguishes the author's proposal from mere populist accommodation, framing it instead as a return to liberalism's original success formula — a positioning relevant to how center-left political strategists might justify policy shifts toward working-class priorities.
insights.quote: my emphasis on the working class is rooted in the fact that liberalism’s current failures are related to its abandonment of the working class and its priorities.

insights.claim: Working-class liberalism, as Acemoglu defines it, has strong communal roots, eschews social engineering, and prioritizes shared prosperity, jobs, and public services, while still requiring liberal safeguards so that communities don't become 'stultifying cages' that restrict individual members' freedom.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Balances communitarian and individual-rights concerns explicitly, providing a template that avoids both technocratic overreach and majoritarian community tyranny — relevant to policy design debates.
insights.quote: Working-­class liberalism has strong communal roots, eschews social engineering, and prioritizes shared prosperity, jobs, and public services.
insights.locator: Working-­class liberalism has strong communal roots

insights.claim: Acemoglu warns that if liberalism fails to remake itself, the alternatives that win out will not be neutral but will include new oligarchies, authoritarianism, ethnonationalism, deep-rooted hierarchy, or renewed extreme progressive movements.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: Sets explicit stakes and a list of specific alternative political outcomes for investors and policymakers to monitor as indicators of liberal-democratic erosion in specific countries.
insights.quote: If liberalism does not remake itself, it will be anti-liberal, anti-democratic alternatives—such as new oligarchies, authoritarianism, ethnonationalism, deep-­rooted hierarchy, or renewed extreme progressive movements—that will win out.
insights.locator: The path ahead is not easy

insights.claim: Acemoglu observes that illiberal movements are already succeeding to a significant extent in many countries, including the United States, by clamping down on speech, trampling the rule of law, dismantling safeguards against abuse of power, and reintroducing hierarchies and inequities.
insights.speaker: Daron Acemoglu
insights.so_what: A direct claim about the present state of democratic backsliding in the U.S. specifically, relevant to political-risk assessments of U.S. institutional stability.
insights.quote: In many countries, including the United States, these attacks have succeeded, at least to a certain extent, and anti-liberal forces are ascendant and are clamping down on speech, trampling on the rule of law, dismantling safeguards against abuse of power
insights.locator: When liberalism fails, illiberal rivals rush in
